No product code is present in this working directory — it holds only the skill library and `CLAUDE.md`. Every count below is yours as reported, not measured by me; §7.3 asks for a script-counted commit tally per component and I could not run one.

## What I found

Three foundation choices came from the starter template and nobody recorded a reason for any of them, so all three are **inherited** — a default nobody chose, not a decision. The document database should **be replaced with a relational one, now (the record calls this MIGRATE)**, because four separate workaround classes you describe — hand-written uniqueness checks, write-conflict retries, joins assembled in application code, readers for old document shapes — are the exact signal set for a relational domain sitting on a non-relational store, and your stated ceiling of tens of small customers sits far inside what one relational node carries. The serverless backend needs **the same component with a different connection setup (ADJUST)**, contingent on the store move. Platform sign-in **stays (KEEP)** and does not have to move with the store.

On timing: now, not after the first customers. Reversal cost rises with every row of real data, and "before the first real data enters an environment" is itself a review trigger — you are standing on the cheapest day this migration will ever have.

## Why it matters

Acting now means the migration is a code rewrite against an empty production store: no backfill under live traffic, no dual-write window, no expand/contract across two paradigms, no customer-visible downtime, no erasure obligations over real employee assessment data. Not acting converts all of that into the migration you will run later with customers attached — and in the meantime one commit in eight keeps buying store workarounds instead of features, and each new hand-written invariant is more code the migration deletes. The honest cost of acting now is feature time spent pre-revenue; at a 1-in-8 platform tax that spend is already happening, just spread out and invisible.

I cannot tell you the migration's size, only its direction. The number below that decides the size is in step 1.

## Do this first

1. **Find out where authorization lives.** If role checks ride on the document store's security rules rather than in the backend, migrating the store also means re-homing every authorization decision into application code — that single fact can double the migration and it is the one thing that could change the "now" answer. Search the store's rules/policy configuration for role and tenant predicates.
2. **Spike one relational candidate for at most a day** (§4.3): the hardest join-and-report query from your domain, plus the erasure-of-one-employee path across store and identity provider.
3. **Write the three records** where decisions already live in this project, then hand the staging to `evolutionary-database-design`.

## What I did not check

- Commit and issue counts per component — closed by running `git log --since=6.months -- <store-access paths> | wc -l` against the real repo, which I do not have here.
- Seven of ten profile dimensions: isolation and residency, data lifecycle and retention, identity federation needs, workload shape, operability, cost envelope, lock-in tolerance. Closed by a `requirements-grounding` quality-characteristic sweep. Employee assessments are likely personal data under a residency and erasure regime; that sweep is not optional before the records are final.
- Whether the store and sign-in are bundled in one vendor platform — closed by reading the infrastructure-as-code and runtime config (§7.1).
- Every walking-skeleton path (§5). None has been run on a relational candidate.

---

```text
Mode:            Review (relational-domain tripwire; before first real data)
Component:       Document database (primary store)
Door:            ONE-WAY
Status:          INHERITED
Forcing need:    None found. No record exists for the original choice.
Profile:         Domain shape: employers, employees, roles, assessments, reports;
                 cross-entity uniqueness, referential integrity, and multi-entity
                 writes all present -> relational. Access patterns: joins across
                 >=3 entities assembled in application code. Scale: tens of small
                 tenants, stated ceiling; inside one node. Isolation/residency GAP.
                 Data lifecycle GAP. Cost GAP. Lock-in tolerance GAP.
Evidence:        Four of six §6 relational-on-document signals present as reported:
                 hand-written uniqueness checks, write-conflict retries, manual
                 joins, readers for old document shapes. Platform tax reported at
                 ~1 commit in 8; NOT VERIFIED by count. No skeleton path run on a
                 relational candidate.
Verdict:         MIGRATE
Tripwires:       Store-touching commit share >12.5% of commits, owner = tech lead,
                 evaluated at monthly review -> escalates migration priority.
                 First real customer record written to production, owner = tech
                 lead, evaluated at release gate -> reversal cost steps up; the
                 cheap window has closed.
Reversal cost:   Today: rewrite of data-access code plus the owned port; no data
                 to move. Raised by: every row of real customer data, every added
                 hand-written invariant, and authorization logic held in store
                 security rules rather than the backend.
Handoff:         evolutionary-database-design (stage the migration);
                 requirements-grounding (close residency, lifecycle, cost gaps)
Next action:     Determine whether authorization is enforced in store security
                 rules or in the backend; that sizes the migration.
```

```text
Mode:            Review (consequence of store verdict)
Component:       Serverless backend (compute model)
Door:            ONE-WAY
Status:          INHERITED
Forcing need:    None found.
Profile:         Workload shape GAP (request/response vs. batch assessment imports
                 and report generation unknown). Scale: tens of small tenants.
                 Operability GAP (team size, on-call). Cost at idle GAP.
Evidence:        NOT VERIFIED. No cold-start, parity, or cost signal reported.
                 Per-invocation connections against a relational store are a known
                 exhaustion mode but unmeasured here.
Verdict:         ADJUST (contingent on the store migration landing)
Tripwires:       Connection-pool saturation or connection-limit errors in any
                 environment, threshold = any occurrence, owner = tech lead,
                 evaluated at the post-migration skeleton run.
                 Idle monthly cost outside envelope, threshold = envelope once
                 defined, owner = tech lead, evaluated at quarterly review.
Reversal cost:   Moderate: consolidating functions into one deployable is a
                 packaging and deploy change, not a data change. Flat over time.
Handoff:         architecture-guidelines (whether the backend may rely on the
                 platform beneath it); ci-cd-reliability-architecture (deploy)
Next action:     Include a connection-pooling strategy in the one-day relational
                 spike; do not treat it as discovered later.
```

```text
Mode:            Review (triggered alongside store review)
Component:       Platform-managed sign-in (identity provider / user store)
Door:            ONE-WAY
Status:          INHERITED
Forcing need:    None found.
Profile:         Identity: employer and employee sign-in, administrative roles
                 implied by the domain. Federation needs GAP. Account lifecycle
                 GAP. Residency of identity data GAP.
Evidence:        NOT VERIFIED. No tripwire reported against identity.
Verdict:         KEEP
Tripwires:       Authorization logic found in the identity platform's rules rather
                 than the application, threshold = any, owner = tech lead,
                 evaluated during the step-1 check -> re-opens this verdict.
                 A customer requires federation (SSO/SAML/OIDC) the platform
                 cannot meet, threshold = first such request, owner = tech lead,
                 evaluated at quarterly review.
Reversal cost:   High and rising with each real user account: credentials usually
                 cannot be exported, so migration means re-enrollment. Lower now
                 than after first customers, but identity need not move with the
                 store.
Handoff:         requirements-grounding (federation and account-lifecycle sweep)
Next action:     Confirm the default holds — the application owns authorization,
                 the provider only authenticates. If sign-in and the document
                 store are one bundled platform, state explicitly that the store
                 migration leaves identity in place.
```
